blocks.prompt: Dinner in the Branches
blocks.text: A leopard hunts at night. Its eyes can see in the dark. Its paws are soft, so it walks with no sound. It sneaks up close before it runs. A leopard is not the biggest cat. A lion is bigger. A hyena will steal a leopard's dinner if it can. So the leopard has a trick. It grabs its food in its jaws and climbs. Up and up it goes, all the way into a tree. Lions do not climb well. Hyenas cannot climb at all. Way up on the branch, the leopard eats in peace.

blocks.prompt: The Cat With a Tree for a Table
blocks.text: A leopard lives alone. It does not hunt in a group the way lions do. Everything a leopard needs, it does by itself: find the food, catch the food, keep the food. That last part is the hard one. Africa is crowded with hungry animals. Lions, hyenas, and wild dogs are all happy to take a meal they did not catch, and a single leopard cannot fight off a pack of them. So the leopard moves its dinner somewhere they cannot follow. It takes the prey in its jaws, sets its claws into the bark, and climbs. A leopard can haul an antelope heavier than itself straight up a tree trunk. Once the meal is wedged in a fork of branches, it is safe. Lions are heavy and clumsy climbers. Hyenas cannot climb at all. The leopard can come back and eat from it for days. Its spots do the rest of the work. They are not solid dots. They are rings called rosettes, and in patchy shade they break the cat's shape into pieces. A leopard can lie on a branch above your head and look like nothing but leaves.

blocks.prompt: The Cat Nobody Sees
blocks.text: No wild cat lives in more places than the leopard. Tigers need forest. Lions need open country. Snow leopards need mountains. The leopard needs almost nothing in particular. It has been found in rainforest and desert, on snowy Russian ridges, in Indian farmland, and on the rocky hills above African towns. Its range once stretched from the Atlantic coast of Africa to the Pacific coast of Asia. The reason is its stomach. A lion is fussy about size, and a leopard is not. Scientists studying leopard droppings have identified more than ninety different animals in the diet, from antelope and monkeys and porcupines all the way down to fish, birds, beetles, and rats. An animal that will eat almost anything can live almost anywhere. It is also very good at not being seen. Leopards move at dusk and at night, alone, and their rosettes dissolve their outline in broken light. This is why leopards live in places people swear they do not. Sanjay Gandhi National Park sits inside the city of Mumbai, home to more than twenty million people, and roughly forty leopards live in it. They come out after dark and hunt the feral dogs and pigs around the edges of the neighborhoods. Most residents never see one. Even the famous black panther is a leopard. It is an ordinary leopard carrying a gene that floods its coat with dark pigment. Hold a light at the right angle and the rosettes are still there, hidden in the black.

blocks.prompt: The Animal Named After a Mistake
blocks.text: For a long time, nobody was sure what a leopard was. The ancient Greeks looked at the spotted cat and decided it had to be a cross between a lion, leon, and a panther, pardos. They welded the two words together, and the animal has carried the mistake in its name ever since. It is not a hybrid. It is Panthera pardus, one of the four big cats that can roar, and the smallest of them. Its roar does not boom like a lion's. It rasps, over and over, like someone slowly sawing a plank of wood. The leopard survives by being unremarkable in the best possible way. It is not the fastest hunter on the savanna, nor the strongest, nor the biggest. What it has is range. Leopards have been recorded in rainforest, desert edge, mountain snow, mangrove, and the outskirts of cities. Researchers who sift through leopard droppings have counted well over ninety prey species, from eland calves down to dung beetles. Specialists starve when their one food disappears. Generalists shrug and eat something else. Its most famous habit follows from a weakness. A leopard hunts alone and cannot defend a kill from a lion pride or a clan of hyenas, so it removes the kill from the argument entirely. Gripping the carcass in its jaws, it climbs a vertical trunk, hauling weight that can exceed its own body mass, and wedges the meal in a fork of branches. Lions are too heavy to follow. Hyenas cannot climb. What began as an act of surrender becomes a pantry that lasts days. And yet. The most adaptable big cat on Earth is now listed as Vulnerable. Leopards have vanished from most of their historic range, squeezed out by farmland, roads, and snares, and hunted for their skins. The Amur leopard, the subspecies that learned to live in the snow of the Russian Far East, was down to a few dozen individuals before protection began pulling it slowly back. Adaptability buys an animal a great deal. It does not buy it space.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Panthera pardus
Widest natural distribution of any wild cat
Generalist diet: 90+ recorded prey species
Caches kills in tree forks, above lions and hyenas
Melanism is a recessive gene, rosettes remain underneath
Around 40 leopards live inside Mumbai
Listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN

blocks.prompt: The Generalist's Trap
blocks.text: Ask which big cat is most likely to be watching you, and the honest answer is the leopard. Not because it is common, but because it is everywhere, and because you will not see it. Panthera pardus has the widest natural distribution of any wild cat. Tigers hold to forest. Lions want open grassland. Cheetahs want room to run. The leopard has been recorded in equatorial rainforest, in desert margin, in the snow of the Russian Far East, in mangrove swamp, in Himalayan foothills, and in the scrub on the edges of enormous cities. The reason is not strength. It is indifference. A leopard is a generalist, and a generalist is nearly impossible to starve. Researchers who examine leopard scat have identified well over ninety prey species: eland calves, baboons, hyraxes, porcupines, fish, birds, hares, dung beetles. Specialists die with their food source. Generalists eat what is left. Its signature behavior grows out of a weakness rather than a strength. A leopard hunts alone. It has no pride behind it and no clan to back it up, and a lioness or a group of hyenas will simply take a carcass away from it. So the leopard removes the carcass from the argument. It clamps the kill in its jaws, digs its claws into bark, and walks up the trunk. Field observers have watched leopards haul prey heavier than themselves into the canopy and wedge it in a fork of branches, out of reach of animals too heavy to climb or unable to climb at all. Surrender, engineered into a pantry. The cat returns to feed for days. The coat is engineering too. A leopard's spots are not dots. They are rosettes: broken rings of black around a patch of coat slightly darker than the background. In steady light a leopard is obvious. In the shifting, broken light under trees at dawn and dusk, exactly the hours it moves, the rosettes fragment its outline into scattered shadow. The black panther of legend is the same animal with a single change, a recessive gene that floods the coat with melanin. The rosettes have not gone anywhere. Angle a light across a black leopard and the pattern rises out of the dark like watermarked paper. All of which sets up the problem. Sanjay Gandhi National Park is an island of forest inside Mumbai, a city of over twenty million people, and around forty leopards live in it. They hunt feral dogs and pigs at night along the edges of neighborhoods, and almost nobody ever sees one. That is a remarkable act of coexistence, and it is also the leopard's trap. A tiger cannot live beside a city. A leopard can, which means the leopard does not get the wide, empty, protected land the tiger is given. It gets farms, roads, snare wire, poison, and the constant risk that a frightened crowd finds it first. The leopard is listed as Vulnerable, gone from most of the range it once held. The Amur subspecies, which learned to hunt in snow, fell to a few dozen animals before protection slowly began to lift it. The lesson is uncomfortable. Being adaptable does not save an animal. It only changes how it is lost: not in one dramatic collapse, but quietly, a farm at a time, in places where people insist there are no leopards left.
